title: Rejoice always (Philippians 4:4–7)
hook: the Lord is near; don't be anxious; the peace that passes understanding

segments.voice: Yesterday, Euodia and Syntyche, and your line was be of one mind. Did you say something good about someone who wasn't in the room? Day six hundred sixty-six.

Three in the morning. The ceiling. The list running in your head: the bill, the test result, the thing you said, the thing you didn't say. Worry is very good at its job. It feels like doing something, and it does nothing. Now consider where these next lines were written. Not from a beach. Paul is in custody, waiting to learn whether he'll live or die. He has just finished asking two friends to stop quarreling. And the next thing he writes is a command to be glad. Not once. Twice.

In the King James Bible: "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice." Note the small words. In the Lord. Paul isn't telling anyone to feel happy about everything that happens. He's pointing at where the joy is anchored. Then: "Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand." Moderation here is gentleness, a kind of give, the opposite of insisting on your rights. And the Lord is at hand can be heard two ways, and both may be meant: he is coming soon, and he is close by right now. Then the line about worry. The King James says: "Be careful for nothing." That sounds like permission to be sloppy, but in the King James's English, careful meant full of care, anxious. Don't be anxious about anything. And instead of worry, a practice: "but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." Every thing. Small things too. And notice with thanksgiving tucked in the middle, like a stone in a shoe. You bring the worry, and you bring a thank-you alongside it. Then the promise: "And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus." The word for keep is a military word. It means to guard, the way soldiers garrison a town. Paul says peace will stand at the gate of the heart. Not a peace that makes sense of everything. A peace that goes past understanding, and holds anyway.
screen: `IN THE LORD: JOY WITH AN ANCHOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring one worry, with thanks. Settle, and breathe. Name one worry, the one most likely to wake you tonight. Say it plainly in your mind, the whole of it, without dressing it up. Then, right beside it, name one thing you're thankful for. It doesn't need to fix the worry. Just set it next to it. Worry, and thanks. If you pray, you can make both known to God, as Paul says, in your own words. If you don't, simply let the two sit together and breathe. Notice if anything at the gate goes quiet. The bell holds the time.
Rejoice always. Paul's double command from prison: rejoice in the Lord, again rejoice, and bring every worry with thanksgiving.
Your line: the peace that passes understanding. Today, every time a worry comes back, add one thanks to it before you put it down. Day six hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Philippians 4:4–7 is read in many churches during Advent, and the words about the peace of God are used as a blessing at the end of services in several traditions, including Anglican worship.

myth: be careful for nothing means don't bother being careful
in the old English, careful meant full of care. it means don't be anxious.
Paul wrote these lines while in custody
he was in chains, waiting to learn his fate, as the letter says.
the word for keep is a military word

fork.setup: it's three in the morning and a worry won't let go. according to Paul, what do you do?
options: think it through until it's solved.
push it away and think of something else.
bring it to God in prayer, with thanksgiving.
fork.reveal: "in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." then peace stands guard.

original.note: Greek: peace. the Greek word often carries the fuller sense of the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, all things well.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful slogan to be happy all the time.
what it means: joy anchored in the Lord, every worry brought with thanks, and a peace beyond understanding.
what a scholar hears: phroureō, to guard like a garrison, written to a Roman colony; and KJV 'careful' in its 1611 sense of anxious.

notes: The carry 'the peace that passes understanding' follows modern wording; the KJV reads 'passeth all understanding'.
φρουρέω (4:7) as a military guard/garrison term; Philippi as a colony settled with Roman veterans. Standard commentary; confirm.
ἐπιεικές (4:5), KJV 'moderation', glossed as gentleness/forbearance. Confirm.
Use of 4:7 as a closing blessing in Anglican and other services, and of 4:4–7 in Advent (e.g. Gaudete Sunday in some lectionaries): confirm the howItsDone wording.
'Be careful for nothing': KJV 'careful' in the older sense of anxious. Confirm.
